mood: Varali has a solemn, ancient, and dignified mood with a strong devotional and contemplative pull. Its vakra ascent and vivadi color give it a serious, weighty emotional atmosphere that can feel prayerful, introspective, and slightly austere. It often evokes reverence, pathos, and a sense of timelessness, making it suitable for compositions of devotion, especially those addressed to deities such as Ganesha and Rama. The raga can also suggest a restrained grandeur rather than overt sweetness.
description: Varali or Varaali (pronounced varāḷi) is a Carnatic rāgam classified either as the 39th melakarta raga or as a janya rāgam of the 39th melakarta Jhalavarali. The source text notes that although it is treated as a melakarta, it is most often rendered with a vakra (zig-zag) ascending scale, making it an asymmetric vakra-sampurna-sampurna rāgam. It is the 4th of the five Ghana rāgams, after Natta, Gaula, Arabhi, and Shree. Historically it was called Varati and is said to be more than 1300 years old, appearing in old musical texts such as Sangita Makarandha and Sangita Ratnakara. The scale uses shadjam, shuddha rishabham, shuddha gandharam, prati madhyamam, panchamam, shuddha dhaivatam, and kakali nishadham. The madhyamam is described as slightly higher than the usual prati madhyamam and is called chyuta panchama madhyamam, also referred to as Varali madhyamam. Some traditions also allow the phrase S R1 G1, which appears in compositions such as Kanakana ruchira. The raga is strongly associated with devotional repertoire, especially compositions in praise of Lord Ganesha and Lord Rama. The text also records a traditional belief that Varali should not be taught directly from teacher to student, but learned by listening and self-study, as direct teaching may strain relationships or cause ill effects.
gamaka_usage: Varali is rendered with a characteristic vakra treatment in the ascent, so the notes are not approached in a straight scalar manner. The source specifically highlights the phrase S R1 G1 as an accepted melodic opening in some traditions, though the more common ascent is S G1 R1 G1 M2 P D1 N3 >S. The raga’s madhyamam is special: it is not the ordinary flat prati madhyamam but a slightly higher chyuta panchama madhyamam (Varali madhyamam), so M2 must be intoned with great precision and a distinct shade. G1 and R1 are central and are typically handled with delicate oscillation and careful slides to preserve the raga’s identity; the zig-zag movement around S, G1, and R1 is essential. The vivadi notes require controlled, nuanced intonation rather than heavy kampita, and the raga’s dignity depends on avoiding overly plain, scalar rendering. Compared with closely related sampurna ragas, Varali’s identity comes from its unusual ascent and the special treatment of madhyamam rather than from broad gamaka excess.
